PreDist Dataset - Operational data of district heating substations labelled with faults and maintenance information
results.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
results.abstract: This dataset consists of operational data and labels based on incident reports and maintenance data of district heating substations of enercity Netz GmbH. The labels are available as a list of ‘disturbances’ as well as a list of fault reports including a short description and problem category, which can be used to develop (early) fault detection models for district heating substations. In addition, fault labels and monitoring potential were added to the reports where possible. The dataset is published together with the paper "Enabling Predictive Maintenance in District Heating Substations: A Labelled Dataset and Fault Detection Evaluation Framework based on Service Data", which explains the dataset in detail. When referring to this dataset, please cite the paper mentioned in the related work section. The PreDist dataset contains time series of 93 district heating substations from two manufacturers, M1 and M2, each time series spanning different lengths of time, depending on when the substation was ‘digitised’. Both sub-datasets contain a list of faults (based on incident reports), a list of disturbances (incident reports, and corrective and preventive maintenance tasks and activities), feature descriptions and a list of pre-defined ‘normal events’, which can be used in addition to the faults to evaluate normal behaviour models.Changes in version 2:A list of all substations with associated configuration type has been added to each manufacturer (file 'configuration_types.csv'). The readme file has been updated accordingly and includes a short description of the different configuration types present in the dataset.

results.title: Optimising District Heating Substations with EnCoDaPy: A Modular Python Framework for Local Control and Energy Management
results.abstract: Increasing demands on district heating networks, coupled with the heat transition in Germany, require innovative operational management strategies. This paper introduces the EnCoDaPy (Energy Control and Data Preparation in Python) framework, which provides modular, real-time and scalable energy management solutions. By integrating with platforms such as FIWARE, EnCoDaPy enables the seamless communication and control of decentralised energy systems. The framework offers a modular configuration, including validation, to facilitate error detection and customisation. A use case involving a district heating substation controller illustrates how the framework can optimise energy efficiency and self-consumption by combining a centralised schedule creation with local implementation. Simulations highlight the benefits of the rule-based approach, while also acknowledging its limitations when it comes to handling complex systems. This suggests that there is a need for the future integration of model-based predictive control. The case study also highlights the potential for optimising the operational management of district heating substations. EnCoDaPy provides a robust foundation for research and industrial applications. Additionally, there are plans for further development and validation.

results.title: Enabling predictive maintenance in district heating substations: A labelled dataset and fault detection evaluation framework based on service data
results.abstract: Early detection of faults in district heating substations is imperative to reduce return temperatures and enhance efficiency. However, progress in this domain has been hindered by the limited availability of public, labelled datasets. We present an open-source framework combining a service-report-validated public dataset, an evaluation method based on accuracy, reliability, and earliness, and baseline results implemented with EnergyFaultDetector, an open-source Python framework developed for automated anomaly detection in operational data from energy systems. The dataset contains time series of operational data from 93 substations across two manufacturers, annotated with a list of disturbances due to faults and maintenance actions, a set of normal-event examples and detailed fault metadata. We evaluate EnergyFaultDetector models, adapted and configured for district heating substations, using three metrics: accuracy for recognising normal behaviour, an eventwise F-score for reliable fault detection with few false alarms, and earliness for early detection. The framework also supports root cause analysis using ARCANA, a feature-attribution method for autoencoders. We demonstrate three use cases to assist operators in interpreting anomalies and identifying underlying faults. The models achieve high normal-behaviour accuracy (0.98) and eventwise F 0 . 5 of 0.83 and could detect 60% of the faults in the dataset before the customer reported a problem, with an average lead time of 3 to 5 days. Integrating an open dataset, metrics, open-source code, and baselines establishes a reproducible, fault-centric benchmark with operationally meaningful evaluation, enabling consistent comparison and development of early fault detection and diagnosis methods for district heating substations.

results.title: Towards automation of fault detection and diagnosis for district heating substations: A three-layer hybrid approach
results.abstract: District heating (DH) networks play a crucial role in achieving climate neutrality goals, but faults in these systems significantly impact energy efficiency. Traditional rule-based fault detection lacks generalization capabilities. Emerging machine learning (ML) techniques frequently suffer from a scarcity of labeled training data. This paper presents a fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) methodology for DH substations that addresses these challenges by significantly automating the setup of the FDD for an individual substation. The focus is on detecting hard faults at the substation level rather than suboptimality in the DH network. The proposed three-layer approach combines ML models, mode-based rules, and rule-based system boundary monitoring. The methodology is validated using measurement data from real-world district heating network substations. A novel kNN-based selection algorithm is introduced to automatically isolate representative training data, addressing a major bottleneck in regression-based FDD. The ML-based FDD then employs regression models to identify deviations from normal operation. For the mode-based FDD, rules derived from the substation control strategy detect faulty operating modes. System boundaries are monitored using defined thresholds. Validation with historical real-world measurements demonstrates the effectiveness of this three-layer approach in detecting various fault types. In two detailed case studies, the FDD framework detected the faults 8.5 h before the presumed technician intervention and 104 h before the customer report, and maintains a low false alarm rate of 0.27% and 0.01%. These findings indicate that the proposed methodology supports scalable, proactive maintenance for district heating substations.

results.title: Pilot-scale hybrid district heating substation integrated with adsorption heat pump
Evaluating Demand-Side Flexibility in District Heating Substations via Offline Reinforcement Learning
results.venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Systems, and Emerging Technologies (ICAISET)
results.abstract: District heating utilities face high peak loads that drive production costs and limit low-carbon integration. In many buildings, time-of-day strategies such as night setback are widely used; they are easy to deploy but cannot adapt to building-specific dynamics. We study whether a simple offline reinforcement learning (RL) approach can learn flexibility-activation policies from historical meter data for individual substations. We train fitted Q-iteration (FQI) with a linear function approximator on hourly heat demand and exogenous features, using a one-step Ridge surrogate to predict next-hour demand under binary comfort actions. Historical actions are inferred as proxy actions from time-of-day labels that approximate a night-setback window. We compare the learned policy against two rule-based controllers (night setback and peak-hour reduction), behavioral cloning, and trivial always-normal and always-reduced policies. All policies are evaluated offline by rolling them out through the surrogate over a held-out winter test period; reported peaks are therefore surrogate rollouts, not field measurements. On a cohort of five real district heating substations in a Nordic climate, screened for data quality and surrogate fidelity, the offline RL policy achieves a median peak reduction of 18.6% (range 12.3%–28.7%) relative to the reconstructed baseline. It matches or outperforms the night-setback rule (RBC A) on four substations and the peak-hour rule (RBC B) on two substations, supporting competitiveness of lightweight offline RL with common rule-based strategies under shared offline evaluation, using only standard metering data and a single global configuration.

results.title: Room Temperature Prediction for District Heating Substation Control: Integrating CatBoost Solar Radiation Prediction and State-Space Modeling
results.abstract: In district heating systems, the large-scale deployment of room temperature collectors has accumulated massive amounts of terminal data, but these data mostly remain at the level of viewing and statistical analysis and have not been effectively connected to real-time control of district heating substations. As a direct reflection of thermal comfort, room temperature can be incorporated into predictive control of district heating substations, which can promote the transition of heating control from lagging compensation to proactive prediction. To address three engineering bottlenecks, namely, the lack of solar radiation information, significant differences in user thermal characteristics, and the accumulation of prediction errors, this paper proposes a rolling room temperature prediction method that integrates CatBoost solar radiation prediction, canonical variate analysis (CVA) subspace identification, and adaptive Kalman filtering. Based on representative users selected by clustering, a model predictive control framework with an alternating iterative solution strategy is constructed to directly serve the closed-loop control of district heating substations. The method relies only on conventional weather forecasts and existing data collected by the heating system, without additional hardware costs. Taking a residential community in Luoyang as an example, there were 490 valid users on the prediction day of 16 December 2024. Using data from the 15 days prior to the prediction day for training and hourly rolling prediction, the root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) for all users were 0.203 °C and 0.146 °C, respectively, and the RMSE under six typical weather conditions remained within 0.21 °C. Online computation only involves low-dimensional matrix operations, and the computational burden is small, demonstrating the potential for deployment on existing controllers of district heating substations and good engineering deployability.

results.title: Improving the temperature performance of district heating substations through two-stage thermal cascading: an assessment across different building typologies, climates and design solutions
results.abstract: Substations are fundamental components for the efficient operation of district heating networks. Cascaded layouts are widely recognized as effective solutions for enhancing substation temperature performance, thereby improving overall network efficiency. Despite their potential, clear and quantitative criteria for their design and operation remain lacking, particularly regarding their effectiveness in future low-temperature networks. Considering the renewed interest in district heating, this study investigates the thermal performance of a cascaded two-stage substation applied to two building typologies across six European climates. Using the average return temperature and the annual volume of water withdrawn from the network as key performance indicators, the results are compared with those of a conventional parallel layout. Results show that the cascaded configuration systematically reduces both the return temperature and the network water withdrawal, with benefits strongly dependent on climatic conditions and the relative share of space heating and domestic hot water in the building load. For the apartment building, reductions in the seasonal return temperature range from 0.9–1.2 °C in cold and continental climates to 4.7 °C in zones with milder winters. Corresponding reductions in annual water withdrawal range from 4.47% to 12.6%. For the office building, the reductions are smaller in cold climates (0.4–0.6 °C and 2.62% to 3.44%) due to the predominance of space heating demand over domestic hot water production. Sensitivity analyses on the size of the low-temperature heat exchanger for domestic hot water show that, in northern climates, performance improvements saturate once its heat transfer area becomes comparable to that of the high-temperature exchanger, with further enlargement yielding only marginal benefits below 1%. Conversely, substantially larger gains are achieved in southern regions. Under the assumption of a fixed total heat transfer area, allocating approximately 50% of this area to the low-temperature stage is identified as the most effective solution. Finally, the transition to lower operating temperatures leads to a slight reduction in the effectiveness of the two-stage configuration, with a more pronounced impact in mild climates. However, the two-stage configuration still outperforms the parallel layout.

results.title: Aftercooling of district heating: Performance of substations with cascading concepts
results.abstract: The use of district heating (DH) is a key technology for a sustainable future, but its efficiency depends on the performance of the local DH substations. Conventional DH substations operate with separate flows for space heating (SH) and domestic hot water (DHW). This study investigates alternative configurations in which SH return flow is cascaded to DHW and vice versa, with the aim of reducing the overall return temperature of the DH flow. Conventional and cascaded substation designs were modelled and simulated using real operational data, and their performances were compared based on their flow-weighted return temperatures. The results show that substations with a single cascade generally performed better than conventional designs, while double-cascade substations provided even greater improvement. Additionally, DHW production efficiency was significantly improved by combining a plate heat exchanger with a single hot water tank. Seasonal variations strongly influenced performance, with return temperature reductions from 1.6 to 3.2 °C in a February week and up to 8.5 to 9.5 °C in a July week (no cascade in July week was possible, since there was no SH demand), compared with conventional DH substations. However, additional cascades result in higher pressure drops, which may pose challenges during peak demand.

results.title: Flexible clustering of substations for accurate and rapid hybrid simulation of district heating
results.abstract: District Heating Networks (DHNs) are crucial to decarbonizing the heat supply sector, with the evolution toward 4th and 5th generation systems offering significant potential for efficiency. However, the increasing complexity of these modern systems makes high-fidelity dynamic thermo-hydraulic simulation computationally intensive, particularly for large-scale networks. These simulations are essential for key applications such as thermal loss prediction, supply temperature optimization, operational planning and during the sizing phase of the network. Recent research has utilized Machine Learning (ML)-based surrogate models to replace substation clusters, reducing spatial complexity and accelerating simulations. Yet, the efficacy of this spatial reduction is highly sensitive to the clusters definition. Poorly selected clusters degrade the surrogate models accuracy and undermine the simulation performance. This paper proposes a flexible, task-driven graph clustering methodology specifically designed for ML-based spatial reduction. We introduce physics-informed distance metrics that encode the primary drivers of ML surrogate model errors. These distance metrics are leveraged within a hierarchical agglomerative clustering framework. The methodology is evaluated across 16 DHNs with diverse topological and thermal characteristics. Our results reveal a clear, generalizable trade-off between simulation accuracy and computational time reduction, allowing the integration of user-preferences. On an independent validation DHN, a high physical accuracy preference yielded a deviation of 6.45 MWh in total thermal energy production estimation (3.76% of total thermal losses within the network), albeit with modest computational gains. Expressing the error relative to thermal losses, rather than total production, provides a more meaningful measure of the spatial reduction’s impact on the key operational objectives. Conversely, a high spatial reduction preference reduced the network from 123 to 5 remaining physical nodes and achieved a 91% decrease in computational time, at the cost of a 45.24 MWh deviation in total thermal energy production estimation, representing 26.37% error relative to thermal losses. These findings demonstrate that the proposed clustering framework provides a robust and flexible tool to calibrate the balance between physical fidelity of the simulation and computational speed across varying DHN generations.

results.title: Energy Efficiency of Using Hybrid Heating Substations in Conditions of Integration of Electricity and Thermal Networks in Urban Neighborhoods. Part 2. Application of Heat Pumps in Layout of Central Heating Substations for Reducing the Return District Heating Water Temperature
results.venue: ENERGETIKA Proceedings of CIS higher education institutions and power engineering associations
results.abstract: Improving the efficiency of heat supply requires the integration of energy systems and the coordination of their operating modes. Hybrid systems combining multiple energy sources and storage technologies are considered a promising means of improving the reliability and sustainability of energy supply. Equipping central heating substations with electric boilers, thermal energy storage systems, and heat pumps provides additional opportunities to balance energy generation and consumption, particularly when surplus electricity is available. This paper presents a design assessment of a vapor-compression heat pump unit (VCHPU) integrated into a central heating substation (CHS) to reduce the district heating return-water temperature. The study is motivated by the need to improve heat supply efficiency, increase the temperature difference between the supply and return pipelines, reduce heat consumption from the district heating network, and create the conditions for the coordinated operation of electrical and thermal networks in urban districts. Operational data obtained from the automated control systems of two central heating substations in Minsk were analyzed. The results show that the domestic hot-water circulation system has a significant effect on the district heating return-water temperature. A VCHPU can be integrated into the domestic hot-water system of a CHS to compensate for heat losses in the circulation loop. This approach separates the heating of cold water from the reheating of the circulation flow and, under the operating conditions considered, can reduce the district heating return-water temperature to 14.2 °C. The greatest effect is achieved at above-zero outdoor temperatures when there is no space-heating demand. The results confirm the need for more detailed calculations that account for the seasonal variation in the coefficient of performance of the heat pump unit, capital and operating costs, and electrical-grid operating conditions.

results.title: From lab to practice: Towards a substation-invariant self-supervised transformer for low-label fault detection in district heating
results.abstract: Automated Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) in District Heating (DH) is essential for reducing return temperatures, improving operational efficiency, and supporting the transition to low-temperature, low-carbon integrated energy systems. Practical deployment remains difficult because labelled fault data are scarce and heterogeneous across domains, while unlabelled operational data are abundant, creating a practical mismatch. To address this, we propose a Self-supervised Time Series Transformer (STST) for low-label FDD using routinely available primary-side measurements. We evaluate the method on six datasets spanning laboratory fault emulations, simulation, and real-world DH networks. The results show that primary-side temperatures contain strong fault-discriminative information, while flow measurements add sensitivity to hydraulically driven faults. The proposed method performs competitively in scarce-label and heterogeneous-field settings, achieving F 1 values between 0.77 and 0.98. Cross-domain experiments indicate that fault-relevant structure is transferable across substations within the same network, although transfer remains asymmetric across networks. Overall, the results suggest that self-supervised pre-training and regularised fine-tuning can improve transformer-based DH fault detection under stricter field conditions, while CNN-based and hybrid baselines remain highly competitive in cleaner or more separable regimes. Practical deployment across new networks, therefore, still requires attention to source–target compatibility, local validation, and remaining domain shift.

results.title: TWO-LEVEL PREDICTIVE CONTROL OF A HEATING SUBSTATION USING AN EDGE FLEXIBILITY AGENT
results.abstract: Introduction. Next-generation district heating relies on demand flexibility, typically induced by dynamic heat prices. Replacing the automation of existing heating substations is costly, whereas a software agent on an edge device can be added above a standard PLC with weather-compensated control, writing only the supply temperature setpoint. This paper determines which measurements and model structure such an agent needs for correct estimates and forecasts, and what its flexibility gives to the consumer and to the network. Materials and Methods. An indirectly connected heating substation was modelled component by component with hydraulically and thermally coupled elements and a single-capacity building model. The baseline is a well-tuned weather-compensated curve. The agent combines a state observer, using return-water and room temperatures, with model predictive control over a 36-h horizon. Costs were decomposed using the building heat balance. Peak-to-minimum price ratios of 1-6 and four weather realizations were simulated, as well as 12-h outages of the agent. Results. With only the return-water temperature, the room temperature estimate is biased by about 2.3 °C and converges no faster than the envelope time constant. Correct forecasts also require as many model disturbances as measurements; the agent's 18-h consumption plan is then more accurate than naive forecasts. At equal comfort the agent uses the same energy as the weather curve, but shifts purchases in time. At a price ratio of 4, the consumer's cost falls by 1.9 ± 0.6 %, and peak-hour purchases by 7.9 ± 2.2 %. A 1-h PLC watchdog removes the comfort impact of an agent outage. Conclusions. An edge agent adds flexibility to energy-efficient weather-compensated control without replacing equipment, provided the room temperature is measured, the model is consistent with the measurements and the PLC remains a fallback. Its value is mainly at the network level.

results.title: Conceptual Dataspace Architecture for District Heating Use Case
results.abstract: Low-temperature district heating networks require accurate demand forecasts and active load control to operate efficiently with reduced supply temperatures and high shares of renewable heat. In practice, however, district heating operators have limited access to real-time data from customer substations and buildings due to privacy concerns, data silos, and lack of interoperability. As a result, operators must apply large safety margins, leading to higher losses and reduced overall system efficiency. This paper proposes a conceptual dataspace architecture based on IDSA-compliant components, the Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC) together with N5GEH, a FIWARE-based IoT platform. The approach enables building owners to securely share selected substation data under strict usage policies, supporting improved forecasting and demand response while maintaining full data sovereignty.
